task_row_model.query: How can I implement thread-safe lazy initialization of a singleton in Java using double-checked locking, and why is volatile needed?

documents.content: Academic analysis of the Java Memory Model explains that without proper memory barriers, writes performed during object construction can be reordered with the reference assignment, so another thread may observe a non-null reference to an incompletely constructed object. Declaring a field volatile establishes a happens-before relationship for reads and writes to that field, preventing reordering of the constructor and the reference store and guaranteeing visibility of the fully constructed object to other threads. The specification changes in Java 5 formalized volatile semantics to address these publication problems. This analysis focuses on visibility and instruction reordering, not on usage patterns or API examples.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides the memory-model rationale: volatile prevents reordering and ensures visibility so partially-constructed instances aren't seen.

documents.content: A practical tutorial describes the double-checked locking pattern for lazy singletons. It shows that the instance field should be declared like: private static volatile Singleton instance;. The getInstance() is implemented by first checking if instance is null; if so, enter a synchronized(Singleton.class) block, check instance again, and if still null assign instance = new Singleton();. After initialization the outer null check lets callers avoid synchronization overhead. The tutorial emphasizes the need for the second null check inside the synchronized block and notes that volatile is required for correctness on modern JVMs.
documents.reasoning_trace: Gives the concrete pattern: volatile declaration, first null check, synchronized block, second null check, assignment; notes performance benefit of avoiding sync after init.

documents.content: A developer blog compares singleton implementations and suggests enums as the simplest, safest approach in many cases, since enum singletons handle serialization and reflection attacks automatically. The post speculates that double-checked locking was a popular micro-optimization in older codebases and warns that naive implementations prior to Java 5 were broken. It includes anecdotal performance numbers for synchronized versus unsynchronized access in high-throughput services but does not provide formal proofs or formal memory-model discussion.
documents.reasoning_trace: Noise: offers alternatives (enum), historical note that pre-Java-5 implementations were broken; not required for answer.

documents.content: Reference entry on the Singleton pattern gives a concise definition: ensure a class has only one instance and provide a global access point. It lists common implementations: eager initialization, lazy initialization with synchronization, and double-checked locking. The entry briefly mentions trade-offs: eager is simple but always creates the instance, synchronized lazy is safe but may have overhead, double-checked locking aims to combine safety with low runtime cost once initialized. It does not go into JVM memory-ordering details.
documents.reasoning_trace: Concise pattern summary and trade-offs; mentions double-checked locking as aiming for safety plus lower post-init overhead.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Declare the instance as private static volatile Singleton instance. Implement getInstance() by first checking if (instance == null); if so, synchronize on the class, check instance==null again, and then assign instance = new Singleton(). The volatile prevents constructor/store reordering and guarantees visibility so other threads cannot observe a partially constructed instance, making double-checked locking correct.
